title: Select Wisely From the Menu of Criticism
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece uses a restaurant-menu metaphor to reframe how people should approach negative feedback: order what looks useful, and leave the rest on the table without guilt. The author acknowledges that taking criticism personally is a nearly universal human reflex, but argues a defensive mindset amplifies the sting unnecessarily. People who grow the most from feedback, the piece claims, deliberately select only the relevant parts of criticism and discard what doesn't apply right now, rather than trying to absorb everything at once. This selective approach, the author argues, is what lets high performers stay open to feedback without becoming defensive or overwhelmed.
points: Taking criticism personally is a near-universal reflex, but a defensive mindset amplifies its sting.
People who benefit most from feedback treat it like a menu, selecting only what's useful right now.
Discarding irrelevant criticism without guilt is framed as a skill, not a failure to listen.
This selective approach reduces defensiveness and makes ongoing feedback easier to receive.
quotes: The more we invest in and feel pride in what we do, the more criticism burns.
A defensive mindset about feedback naturally amplifies the need to protect ourselves.
People who most benefit from feedback and criticism take a Menu approach to what they are offered.
Those who grow from criticism take what they need from it and discard the rest.
When learners take what they need from criticism to make their performance better and discard the rest, they find themselves less defensive to negative feedback.
